summary: Report No. 31 of South Korean Interim Government Activities (USAMGIK), prepared by the National Economic Board, covers April 1948, the month before the 10 May election. It records 94% voter registration (7,730,000), 939-942 candidates for 200 seats, communist sabotage and the Cheju revolt, and the Pyongyang North-South conference rejected by American authorities. Economic sections show higher industrial and anthracite output, stable prices, a trade balance turning to export surplus, record rail freight, rising deposits and a revenue surplus. Political chapters cover KILA's de facto dissolution, amnesty for 3,000 political prisoners, police reform, the draft civil code and land sales. Vested-property policy, refugee flow of 15,848, Korean schools in Japan, youth and women's organizations and literacy gains are also documented. Historians will find dense tables, official framing of the election period and detailed reporting on Property Custody and agrarian reform.
highlights: 94% of eligible voters (7,730,000) registered for the 10 May election despite communist terror.
Pyongyang North-South conference opened 19 April; Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic attended; rejected the South-only election.
Cheju-do revolt broke out, mixing communist opposition to the election with feuds against police.
About 3,000 political prisoners amnestied; police now need court warrants for arrests.
Anthracite output reached 62,796 tons, up 49.5% from February, mostly from one rehabilitated mine.
28% of vested farmland sold to Korean farmers in the first month of the program.
April exports exceeded imports by about 15% versus a 1,000% import excess a year earlier.
KILA adjourned for 30 days on 19 April, effectively dissolving itself after passing 11 Public Acts.

sections.title: Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 31 (April 1948), prepared by the National Economic Board; a map; organization charts of USAMGIK and SKIG as of 1 January 1948; notes describing the dual American-Korean apparatus; the NEB roster headed by Dr. Wilhelm Anderson; and a six-part table of contents.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Thirteen numbered paragraphs: 7,730,000 voters (94 percent) registered for the 10 May election despite communist terror; the Cheju revolt; the Pyongyang conference and a Soviet-style constitution; over 15,000 refugees; 28 percent of Japanese farmland sold; stable prices; higher output; trade balance; and literacy rising from 21 to 71 percent.

sections.title: Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Population and foreign affairs; vested property.

sections.title: Section 1: Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Refugee inflow rose 20% over March; Korean League in Japan purged of dissenters; Japan closed non-conforming Korean schools.

sections.title: Population Migration
sections.summary: Refugee entries from North Korea in April reached 15,848, 20 percent above March, as Russians tightened travel limits. Officials inspected the Kaesong camp on 19 April, where refugees stay about three days. The Kyonggi-do quota was shared among five provinces so Inchon could process 2,000 Mukden repatriates. Cumulative inbound total was 2,384,553 against 886,203 outbound.

sections.title: Korean League in Japan
sections.summary: The Office of Foreign Affairs reported that a minority in the Korean League in Japan, trying to end communist domination, was defeated and expelled by leftist leaders following the party line. The League's ideals were Korean nationalism, equal rights with Japanese and foreign-national privileges; its aggressive demands drove dissenters to form separate political groups.

sections.title: Korean Education in Japan
sections.summary: Conflict over Korean schools in Japan peaked in April. Osaka ordered 19 non-compliant schools closed by 15 April, and 14 kept teaching. In Hyogo, 73 parents petitioning the governor were arrested on 15 April; about 4,000 Koreans protesting on 18 April were dispersed by police. A USAMGIK liaison officer urged cooperation with SCAP-directed policy.

sections.title: Section 2: Vested Property
sections.summary: Office of Property Custody: financial statements, guaranteed bank loans, disposal rules for small businesses and residences, claims procedure, audits and rentals.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The Office of Property Custody had two main developments in April: operations centered on the Forms 20 and 21 financial statements arriving from supervised industries, and a standard set of rules for disposing of vested property was published widely. Provincial liaison and training improved, policy memoranda were issued, and 21 chemical plants were inspected.

sections.title: Operations
sections.summary: Operations received 895 financial forms in April, with 519 tabulated showing a net loss of 389.5 million won before taxes. Inspections found paper mills limited by fuel and parts shortages and 21 chemical plants under 30 percent of capacity. A forestry custody order was issued, 6,600 thousand won of capital spending approved, and 51 loan cases totaling 2,138 million won tabulated.

sections.title: Property Disposal
sections.summary: Publicity restated rules for selling Japanese small businesses and residences: managers or occupants get first chance, appraisals precede sales, inadequate bids may be rejected, and all-Korean advisory committees review buyers. Terms required 20 percent down, 5-7 percent interest and contracts up to 10 years. April sales completed numbered 96, worth 62.4 million won.

sections.title: Real Estate Section
sections.summary: The Real Estate Section handled 19 transfers of Army-released property in April, two to SKIG agencies and six covering 180 Seoul houses, and processed 21 Army requisitions. It also drew up a plan for transferring Army real property to the Korean government through OPC, with provincial custodians as representatives, should USAFIK withdraw.

sections.title: Policies and Precedents
sections.summary: The Policy Division issued a statement that property registered to Allied nationals on 9 August 1945 is not vested, but the Custodian will protect it and account for income in the owner's absence. A procedural memorandum covered management and return. Further papers addressed ending brothel use of vested properties and barring lease of critical industrial assets.

sections.title: Claims Section
sections.summary: On 17 April the Military Governor signed a directive simplifying disposal of ownership claims against vested property. Of over 50,000 claims under Ordinance No. 33 handled by the Justice Department's commission, only 50 were processed in a year. The new eight-step expedited procedure, using Korean lawyers, sometimes reached 12 cases a day.

sections.title: Audit Division
sections.summary: The Audit Division completed audits of seven organizations (three commercial associations, two provincial offices) plus five investigation reports and a Korean Industrial Shipbuilding Association balance sheet. It reported 922 desk audits requested and 52 completed. Audit work was decentralized to provincial offices, with balance-sheet audits replacing detailed ones and a field audit section being formed.

sections.title: Property Rentals
sections.summary: A report on rentals as of 1 January 1948 counted 102,822 leases on 82,339 properties, 3.4 percent leased to government employees and 83 percent with rent increases. Tables showed arrears (21.4 percent delinquent, 87.2 million won), gross collections of 319.3 million won since liberation yielding net revenue of 283.5 million, and property types led by 56,080 residences.

sections.title: Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Agriculture, prices, industry, mining, allocation, trade and labor.

sections.title: Section 1: Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Fertilizer sales through KAA rose to 35,091 tons; livestock recovery; silk grading; forest, fisheries and land-sale activities.

sections.title: Agricultural Economics Bureau
sections.summary: The new Crop Reporting Service integrated 281 more persons in April, bringing appointments to 664 as of 20 April, with Cholla-pukto and Kyongsang-namdo complete. Training for gun agricultural statisticians began in Kyonggi-do and spread to other provinces. A grain inspectors' school at Yongdungpo graduated 200 under Order No. 4.

sections.title: Agriculture Production Bureau
sections.summary: Livestock numbers rose steadily from 1946, with 1949 estimates higher. Seoul milk plant lacked ammonia and lost 30 percent of milk; sheep stations were dropped. USGS arranged 400 tons each of sulphur and copper sulphate from Japan. Cotton and hemp goals were set, exportable silk graded poorly, and coal and cement arrived for irrigation work.

sections.title: Bureau of Forestry
sections.summary: Forest output for January and February 1948 was 39,660 and 36,092 cubic meters of logs, 4,423 and 3,719 tons of charcoal, and 314,150 and 198,362 cubic meters of fuelwood. With warm weather the fuel situation eased, Seoul fuelwood falling from 4,000 to 2,500 won per cubic meter. Forest nurseries received 222 tons of ammonium nitrate.

sections.title: Bureau of Fisheries
sections.summary: Processed marine products for 1947 totaled 54,870 metric tons, 3,736 below 1946 and 10,000 under the goal, blamed on shortages of tinplate, salt and transport. Salted fish (27,388 tons) and dried fish (20,874) led. A 14-vessel deep-sea expedition from Pusan landed 389 tons, bringing the program total to 615 tons worth over 26 million won.

sections.title: Korea Agricultural Association
sections.summary: Fertilizer sales to farmers rose in April on seasonal demand and a KAA campaign: 38,464 tons imported and 35,091 sold. From July to 10 April, 306,895 tons were received and 75 percent sold. KAA also collected 839.7 million won, and its straw bag and rope collection exceeded quotas, with 22.2 million bags bought.

sections.title: Agricultural Improvement Service
sections.summary: The service investigated farmer complaints that 20 organizations in the two Kyongsang provinces levied unexplained fees, and an executive order was expected. Maj.-Gen. Dean told provincial officials AIS would unify research, teaching and extension. Experiment station projects were approved, forage land was prepared at two livestock farms, and extension agents agreed to use village discussion clubs.

sections.title: National Land Administration
sections.summary: Sale of former Japanese farmland under Ordinance No. 173 moved quickly: by 30 April, 168,735 of 587,974 farms (28.7 percent) were sold and 8.6 percent had sales binders. Buyers were capped at two chungbo, tenants had preference, price was three times annual crop output, and payment was 20 percent of crop in kind for 15 years.

sections.title: Section 2: Prices
sections.summary: Retail prices in Seoul and nine centers eased slightly in April; wholesale prices nearly unchanged; controlled price lists.

sections.title: Retail and Wholesale Prices
sections.summary: Retail prices in Seoul and nine cities slipped seasonally in April, except Korean turnip, salt, cotton shirting and coal briquettes. Wholesale prices were nearly unchanged: dried fish, yellow hemp, lumber, cement and coal rose, while cleaned rice, cotton yarn, charcoal, firewood, copper and leather fell. Tables gave indexes (August 1945=100) and won prices; Seoul rice retailed at 1,320 won per mal.

sections.title: Controlled Prices
sections.summary: The National Price Administration sets prices for goods from vested or government-controlled enterprises and for Civilian Supply imports. The March 1948 schedule listed controlled prices with effective dates, for example cleaned rice 280 won per large mal, cotton sheeting 56 won per yard, lump anthracite 3,500 won per ton, and calf leather shoes 1,660 won. A chart tracked price and production trends.

sections.title: Section 3: Industrial Production
sections.summary: March output up sharply: cotton yarn 28.5%, cloth 26.2%, paper 36.1%, nails 19.3%, oxygen 80%; rubber shoe reporting widened.

sections.title: Processed Food
sections.summary: Processed food output: the Taihan mill and six small private mills produced 2,386 tons of flour in March, 3.1 percent above February and 28.7 percent above the 1947 monthly average, while a second large mill was being rehabilitated. Six of nine small mills made 628 tons. Noodle output was 77 tons, far below the seasonal average.

sections.title: Textiles
sections.summary: Cotton yarn output in March rose 28.5 percent over February to 522,000 kg, the best since June 1947. Cotton cloth rose 26.2 percent to 2,286,000 meters despite power shortages, one mill getting 300 KW daily against 1,000 KW needed. Mill activity depended on electricity and coal, and cotton distribution to mills remained unreliable.

sections.title: Paper
sections.summary: Machine-made paper from 14 mills hit a post-liberation record of 533.4 metric tons in March, against 391.9 in February. Puksun mill exceeded its best Japanese-era month by 16 percent, and Dai Dong reached a new high. The Dai Yang mill made trial runs, and the first independent ground wood mill, near Seoul, began experiments.

sections.title: Hardware
sections.summary: Nail production in March was 148.9 metric tons, 19.3 percent above February's 124.8 and close to the 1947 monthly average of 142.1. The three plants in South Korea reported fairly steady operations. The table gave monthly output from October 1946, with January 1948 at 150.4 tons.

sections.title: Chemicals
sections.summary: Chemicals in March: briquettes rose 41.3 percent to 6,398 tons, under a third of March 1947, for lack of pitch; no cement made because storage was full, though 1,710 tons of clinker were; common brick resumed at 10,000 tons; rubber shoes reached 1,899,834 pairs with wider coverage; oxygen rose to 90,455 cubic meters; matches and soap noted.

sections.title: Miscellaneous
sections.summary: Miscellaneous output for March: electric insulators fell to 5,512 pieces from 11,760 in February because coal was scarce, while lead pencils rose to 4,521 gross, continuing an upward trend since the start of 1948 (3,089 in January and 3,684 in February).

sections.title: Monopoly Bureau Products
sections.summary: Government salterns produced 16,036 tons in April, nearly three times April 1947, aided by weather and better control; private salterns made 154 tons. Cigarette output fell 17.6 percent in March to 288.8 tons after a week's shutdown for lack of endless tape; the tape factory moved to Seoul and began production on 18 March. Cut tobacco rose to 686.6 tons.

sections.title: Section 4: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output jumped to 62,796 tons from one rehabilitated mine; Japanese bituminous coal imports; pitch and other minerals.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The Bureau of Mining was beginning to realize its coal rehabilitation goal. Anthracite output expanded sharply in March, and April bituminous imports from Japan nearly matched February's record. Total coal supply from March production and April imports was nearly double the tonnage available three months earlier.

sections.title: Indigenous Anthracite and Lignite Coal
sections.summary: Anthracite output rose 49.5 percent in March to 62,796 tons, nearly all from the Samchuk mine (40,596 tons), helped by restored power. Lignite reached 5,112 tons. Under half of the coal reached market, with 53,000 tons stranded at railheads. Hwasun mine was caving, Yong Wol made 10,250 tons in April, and April allocations went to Army, Commerce and railroads.

sections.title: Bituminous Coal
sections.summary: Bituminous coal imports from Japan, the only source, were 83,171 tons in April, nearly equal to February's record 83,330. The railroads received 58,150 tons but reportedly needed at least 100,000 monthly. The Department of Commerce received 7,500 tons, of which 3,520 went to gas and coke plants and 1,000 to cement.

sections.title: Shipments to Consumers
sections.summary: Tonnage delivered to consumers does not match production, import and allocation figures, mainly because of pilferage in transit and because the transport system could not haul all allocated coal. In March 36,659 tons of anthracite and 51,983 tons of bituminous coal were actually supplied.

sections.title: Pitch
sections.summary: Coal tar pitch, needed as binder for briquettes, was virtually unavailable in March, so briquette output was little better than one-third of the 1947 monthly average. Pitch had been ordered from the United States but was not expected for two months. It is good for combustion but too expensive for extensive use.

sections.title: Other Minerals
sections.summary: Gold, valued near 10 million dollars in 1942, remains far from rehabilitated; five Bureau of Mining teams visited over 30 vested gold properties and found 683 stamps in 70 mills producing about 20,000 grams monthly with 3,500 miners. Kobayashi Mining planned ferro-tungsten recovery of 10 tons monthly. Tables gave March output of gold, silver, copper, tungsten, graphite, zinc and lead.

sections.title: Section 5: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: Consumer Goods Allocation Board procedure, civilian supply allocations, petroleum, salt, and allocation and distribution of Korean-produced commodities.

sections.title: Consumer Goods Allocation Board
sections.summary: The National Consumer Goods Office completed and distributed its Standard Operating Procedure, summarizing Executive Order No. 12 and the steps in allocating, distributing and reporting consumer goods. Conferences with G-4, XXIV Corps agreed that incentive goods for service employees go directly to unit commanders where employee co-operatives exist; otherwise the Federation of Financial Associations distributes.

sections.title: Allocation of Civilian Supplies
sections.summary: Civilian Supply, Commerce and Price Administration agreed that miscellaneous supplies from Pusan would be priced against inventory and reconciled later with shipping documents, which lag two to three months, easing Yongdungpo warehouse congestion. DIS surplus clothing and mess equipment was inventoried for re-allocation. April allocations included 4,555 bales raw cotton, 1,500 tons rubber, 78,980 bags cement and 500 cases each of radio batteries.

sections.title: Petroleum
sections.summary: Petroleum Distributing Company April allocations were 6,414,345 liters gasoline, 3,815,507 kerosene, 2,924,821 diesel and 4,242,796 Navy Special fuel oil, with departmental shares for Transportation, Coast Guard, Marine Transportation and electric power. Sales tables show 1947 gasoline at 60,977 thousand liters. Kerosene, diesel and lubricant shortfalls were explained; an anti-illegal-sales ordinance was drafted and the Inchon pipeline to Wangemiri neared completion.

sections.title: Salt Distribution
sections.summary: The Monopoly Bureau reported 25,803 metric tons of salt distributed in April 1948, with 60,812,947 kilograms in stock for May. Home soya-sauce rations of 2.7 kg per person took 21,169,282 kg, fisheries curing 3,268,020 kg, industrial uses 718,596 kg and miscellaneous users such as hotels, restaurants and police mess halls 631,287 kg.

sections.title: Allocation of Korean-Produced Commodities
sections.summary: On 15 April the Consumer Goods Allocation Board unanimously set a 40 per cent government and vested-industry employee share and 60 per cent public share, up from 30-70. Goods worth 12,000,000 won from the former Civil Service Welfare Committee were allocated to 33 organizations. Tables give April allocations totaling 766,082 thousand won across 446 allocations, and monthly cloth, shoe, tire, soap, match, cement, oil and nail allocations.

sections.title: Distribution of Korean-Produced Commodities
sections.summary: The 1947 year-end bonus distribution continued, with 41,000,000 won of goods bought, 96 per cent of the Commerce allocation; 7,828,235 won of goods could not be purchased for stated reasons. The FFA distribution contract was completed 23 April: FFA receives 15 per cent, pays FDA eight, and retailers earn 13 per cent. Tables list 462,505 eligible employees and FFA purchases of 1,628,036 thousand won since July 1946.

sections.title: Section 6: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: April licenses show exports (443.8 million won) exceeding imports (376.8 million won) by about 15%, against 1,000% excess of imports a year earlier.

sections.title: Private Trade Statistics
sections.summary: Licenses issued in April (113 import, 94 export) indicate exports of about 443.8 million won against imports of 376.8 million, a marked improvement from April 1947. March private imports reached 822.7 million won, led by rubber, cotton and newsprint; exports of 654.1 million consisted of dried fish, agar, ginseng and furs. Over 93 per cent of exports went to Hong Kong; Inchon took 62 per cent of imports.

sections.title: Private Trade Activities
sections.summary: Private trade with Hong Kong in April was carried by vessels including the Coastal Buccaneer, Suchow, Kutsang, Choysang and Lenverett. Arrivals at Pusan and Inchon brought paraffin wax, caustic soda, rubber, paper, truck tires and 213 tons of wool. Outbound cargoes were cuttle fish, marine and vegetable products, dried fish and furs, such as 500 tons on the Suchow.

sections.title: Government-to-Government Transactions
sections.summary: Government trade involved a pending offer of 75 tons of lead bullion to a New York firm. Exports to Japan credited to the USAMGIK account were $351,976 for April and $4,223,237 for January-April, led by graphite, zinc concentrates, anchovies and lead. SCAP's offer of six cents per pound for hemp waste was accepted. Pusan shipped 4,242 tons; 427 tons of inferior kaolin were returned.

sections.title: Korean Items for Americans in Korea
sections.summary: Sales of Korean-made goods to the Army Exchange Service in Korea were $27,355 in April, bringing the total since the program began in August 1947 to $174,506. The table shows 17,434 pieces delivered in April, against 22,176 pieces worth $38,746 in March and the 1947 total of 66,065 pieces worth $64,701.

sections.title: Civilian Supply Imports
sections.summary: April civilian supply imports included 83,171 metric tons of coal (286,196 for the year), 47,815 tons of fertilizer with a record 15,551 tons of ammonium sulphate from Japan, and rice only (6,226 tons from the U.S., 3,593 from the Philippines). Salt imports totaled 19,515 tons; petroleum dipped slightly. Cotton, wool, rubber, petroleum coke, cement and medical supplies also arrived.

sections.title: Section 7: Labor
sections.summary: May Day permit dispute, threatened Seoul Electric streetcar strike, labor laws, labor education, industrial health, labor distribution.

sections.title: Labor Union Activities
sections.summary: Chung Pyung's complaint over a May Day permit was referred to General Dean. Dean warned that no illegal Seoul Electric strike would be tolerated and appointed an eight-member fact-finding committee, which recommended reorganizing company management and a union election before June. Marine Bureau and Korea Transportation contracts were negotiated, Pusan stevedores sought rates, and Tai Han won 366 of 413 votes.

sections.title: Labor Laws
sections.summary: The Bureau of Labor Standards found Samchok mines had violated the Maximum Working Hours Law (Ordinance No. 121) until September 1947, and Korean Broadcasting Company workers withdrew overtime claims. Seoul ration stores were exempted from the 60-hour limit during the election emergency. Child Labor Law inspections covered the Tobacco Monopoly and Pyung Chang Silk factories, and minors under 14 in government offices were ordered dismissed.

sections.title: Labor Education
sections.summary: The Bureau of Labor Relations displayed an exhibit on American labor conditions and distributed the November 1946 Industrial Labor Force and Wage Survey. It planned educational tours to six towns in Kangwon-do and Chungchong-pukto using films, slides and speeches. It circulated 7,500 copies of the March Labor News and presented four Monday radio broadcasts of the Laborers' Hour on HKA.

sections.title: Industrial Health
sections.summary: The Industrial Health and Safety Section began a recreation program for 200 girl workers, studied the Japanese industrial accident compensation act, and gave 6,615 immunizations at five Seoul firms. Mine inspections in Kangwon-do (Machari, Sang Dong, Yongwol) produced 43,969 immunizations and found poor hospitals, spoiled meat rations, silicosis and tuberculosis, prompting shipments of drugs, a refrigerator and beds.

sections.title: Labor Distribution
sections.summary: The Department of Labor withdrew its special labor officers from refugee collection camps at Uijongbu and Kaesong, where they had been selecting skilled workers for the provinces. Of 424 workers distributed during 1947, only 60 proved skilled, so the project was judged useless and abandoned in the interest of economy.

sections.title: Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation, communications, utilities and public works.

sections.title: Section 1: Transportation
sections.summary: Shipping priority system adopted; March revenue up 119%; railroads carried 480,000 tons, a record since October 1945.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Rising demand for marine shipping led the Department of Transportation in April to set a priority system for cargo space: 48 per cent for Pusan allotments, 24 coal, 19 rice, six fertilizer from Yosu and three miscellaneous. The plan runs 60 days, after which priorities may be adjusted depending on the overall situation.

sections.title: Revenue and Expenditures
sections.summary: Department of Transportation revenue for March rose 119 per cent, or 283,000,000 won, the highest monthly figure of F/Y 1947/48, partly through 161,000,000 won paid by the U.S. Army for freight and passenger bills and partly through greater rail and marine activity. Expenditures rose too because of fiscal year-end contract payments, reaching 464,552 thousand won against revenue of 520,065 thousand.

sections.title: Railroads
sections.summary: Anti-sabotage precautions kept April damage small. March railroad receipts rose 269,000,000 won, passengers by 921,000, and freight reached over 480,000 tons, the most since October 1945. Operable locomotives rose by 17, and backshop repairs and coal consumption increased. Employment kept falling but wages were the year's highest; Ensung coal was being tested in locomotives.

sections.title: Marine Transportation
sections.summary: Marine receipts for March were 147 per cent above February because of heavier traffic and higher rates, and expenditures rose with year-end payments. Employment rose slightly to 2,540. At Pohang, dredging let FS-type ships enter the harbor, while dredging continued at Kunsan and Mokpo and work began to remove Japanese crane wreckage at Yosu.

sections.title: Highway and Air Transportation
sections.summary: Highway Transportation expenditures fell sharply to 356 thousand won in March, partly from year-end lack of funds, while Air Transportation outlays rose nine per cent to 296 thousand won. Neither bureau reported income. Highway employment stood at 72 and air employment at 31 in March.

sections.title: Section 2: Communications
sections.summary: Communist sabotage shifted to Cheju (16 poles cut, 26 wires cut); revenue, employment, postal savings, telephone and broadcasting.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The communist sabotage campaign against communications on the mainland waned in April, but an intensive drive hit Cheju island: 16 telephone poles were cut down and 26 wires cut. Other provinces suffered slight damage. In Kwangju, telephone and telegraph employees rioted and partly interrupted service for more than 24 hours.

sections.title: Revenue and Expenditures
sections.summary: Department of Communications revenue rose markedly in March: telephone fees up 14,000,000 won, insurance up 2,000,000 won from year-end bills, and stamps up 1,000,000 won with new issues. Postal, radio and telegraph fees fell 5,000,000 won because provincial reporting was incomplete. Expenditures dropped over 50 per cent to 39,282 thousand won for lack of fiscal year-end funds.

sections.title: Employment
sections.summary: Employment in the Department of Communications continued to decline in March, to 13,113 from 13,479 in February, in compliance with the Military Governor's reduction-in-force orders. Postal staff fell to 3,292 and insurance staff to 871, while telephone staff stood at 3,068.

sections.title: Special Functions
sections.summary: Government income collected by Communications for the Department of Finance rose over 39 per cent in March to 726 million won, the high point since October 1945. Monopoly returns were higher because cigarette factories ran the full month rather than 20 days, and taxes on other products stayed high, with taxes reaching 704 million won.

sections.title: Postal Deposits and Insurance
sections.summary: In March the Postal Deposit System gained 1,868 depositors, reaching 7,002 thousand, and deposits rose 562,170 won, holding at 843 million. The Postal Book Transfer System lost depositors (52,828) but deposits were 31,000,000 won above February at 154 million. National Life Insurance policies fell to 5,308 thousand, though insurance in force rose 6,000,000 won to 1,776 million.

sections.title: Telephone and Telegraph
sections.summary: Telephone messages in March were 17,000 above February at 182,000, with revenue up 739,000 won to 11,464 thousand won. Telegraph traffic and revenue also rose: domestic messages sent were 182,215 and domestic revenue 6,691,343 won, while messages to Japan generated 92,739 won.

sections.title: Korean Broadcasting Corporation
sections.summary: Effective 15 April, the license fee for Korean civilian owners of entertainment radio receivers rose from 40 won to 50 won per month.

sections.title: Communications Bureau
sections.summary: The Seoul-Pusan telephone circuit of the Korean Electric Power Company was re-aligned 20 April, and a radio station at Mukko, Kangwon-do was costed for the Bureau of Mines. Inspections of Seoul plants (Chosun Light Industry, Chosun Communications Industry, Chosun Electric Industry) surveyed capacity to make telephone plugs, switchboard parts and 20 constabulary radio transmitters.

sections.title: Postal Bureau
sections.summary: Two new Korean postage stamps went on sale 10 April: a pink 20-won stamp showing the Independence Gate (one million printed) and a light brown 50-won stamp showing Admiral Yi's Turtle Ship (500,000 printed). Both measure 20 by 24 mm.

sections.title: Section 3: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Electric power 75.9 million KWH in April, with 33.7 million from southern sources; Emergency Power Board, plants, streetcars, power barges.

sections.title: Electricity Distribution
sections.summary: Electricity delivered in April totaled 75,900,000 KWH, slightly below March, with 42.2 million from north of 38 degrees and 33.7 from the south. Lengthening daylight reduced consumption, delivery and service improved and stoppages fell. For the first time, compiled data showed production of all South Korean plants since August 1945, previously a business secret, with seasonal variation similar to U.S. patterns.

sections.title: Emergency Power Board Transactions
sections.summary: The Emergency Electric Power Board met 7 and 21 April on conservation, priorities and allocation if North Korean power were cut off. Unauthorized uses, estimated at 30 per cent of supply, were blamed on big bulbs, floor heating and bypassed cut-offs. Adviser Roames outlined Korean-run load dispatching, backfeeding for water pumps, three 5,000 KVA transformers from Japan, and an interconnected Seoul system.

sections.title: Power Plants
sections.summary: April plant operations were generally favorable. Chung Pyung hydro averaged 15,700 KW, Sumjingang 8,700 KW (third highest ever), Unam did not operate, Yong Wol steam averaged 7,200 KW while stockpiling 4,500 tons of coal, and the Pusan floating plant about 6,500 KW. Japanese engineers repaired a Chung Pyung transformer, and tests showed Dong In Ri can generate 18,000 KW continuously.

sections.title: Street Railways
sections.summary: Seoul streetcars ran about 135 cars in April, with a wage study submitted to the Wage Stabilization Committee and more welfare work. Fred Simons's study settled a dispute over 27,909,000 won in claimed taxes owed by Seoul Electric to the City: traffic tax claim invalid, vehicle and rail taxes due, payable in monthly installments without penalty.

sections.title: Auxiliary Power Barges
sections.summary: The 20,000 KW power barge YFP-1, a former 5,000-ton freighter, was berthed in Pusan Harbor in April under the 11th Medium Port and began producing at once, the first floating plant of its kind. The Navy barge Electra, with six 800 KW diesel generators and 3,000-4,000 KW expected output, reached Inchon for connection to Seoul Electric lines.

sections.title: Section 4: Public Works
sections.summary: Comprehensive spring inspection; no national road appropriation, so volunteer labor carried road, bridge, levee and fire-control work.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: April, the start of the new fiscal year, brought the most detailed inspection of Public Works construction sites yet, showing progress despite funding shortages. Volunteer labor on road, bridge and irrigation work increased, and new volunteer fire companies were installed. Long- and short-range water supply projects advanced and problems found were promptly addressed.

sections.title: Highways
sections.summary: Employment and expenditures on highways were nearly nil in April because no national road appropriation existed, partly offset by volunteer labor. Surveys covered the 54-km Chungdong-ni to Changpyong-ni stretch of the planned Seoul-east coast highway, the Kangnung-Samchok mine road with two unsafe bridges, and the half-repaired Yongwol-Chungju-Chochiwon road.

sections.title: Bridges
sections.summary: Bridge work proceeded well: the Andong bridge was 20 per cent complete at a cost of 4,478 thousand won, and a contract was let 22 April for a concrete deck on the Waegwan bridge, due by July. Capt. Nelson's Namjong Bridge redesign cuts load from 13 to eight tons, saving 5,000 bags of cement and 3,500,500 won. Standard culvert designs were drafted.

sections.title: Irrigation and Flood Control
sections.summary: A new Water Resources Committee under Choi Kyong-wol met 2 and 23 April to coordinate irrigation and flood plans, and began reviewing the Sum Jin Gang dam. Provincial levee projects were reported in Cholla-namdo and Chungchong-namdo, and bulldozer levee work was observed near Seoul. An adviser's flood report cited 311 rivers, the 1946 flood and 1,250,000 feet of needed levees. Tables list projects and costs.

sections.title: Urban Water Supply
sections.summary: The City Planning Bureau drew up the 1948/49 water works program and minimum operating requirements for major cities. Power failures and uneven voltage were the main problems, and Seoul's Duksum pumping station was repaired quickly. A Kolang reservoir was designed, and the Utilities Commission approved Seoul rate increases up to 80 times 1937 levels, about 25 won per seven cubic meters.

sections.title: Maps and Surveys
sections.summary: The Bureau of Geodetic Survey studied the accuracy of the 1:50,000-scale maps of South Korea for possible revision and compiled a tabulation of all triangulation points with latitude, longitude and azimuths. The pages also hold the flood control programs table (4,866 million won to complete, 69,500 hectares) and the proposed 1948/49 water works expenditure figure.

sections.title: Fire Control
sections.summary: April saw 144 fires with 76,018,490 won in estimated losses, one-fifth of March's; January-April totaled 693 fires and 925,350,840 won. A survey found all but five of Seoul's 32 fire lanes passable. A Yongdungpo firm produced 1,200 yards of hose, equipment programs and standardization began, and a 250-member volunteer brigade in Song Tong was recognized 4 April.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: On 3 April the Department of Public Works' Heavy Equipment School at Ascom City graduated its second class of 86 Korean engineers, who completed a three-month course in heavy-equipment operation and management held 12 February to 3 April under the Technological Training Board.

sections.title: Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Government and non-government finance.

sections.title: Section 1: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue fell 5,213 million won from December's 33,389 million; revenue exceeded expenditure second month running.

sections.title: Note Issue of the Bank of Chosun
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun note issue peaked at 33,389 million won in December 1947, mostly from the rice collection, and had fallen 5,213 million by the end of April (28.2 billion won in the table). Causes included completed rice collection and distribution, record tax collections and tobacco sales, little government spending, and 1,132 million won of deposit transfers during April.

sections.title: Overdraft to South Korean Interim Government
sections.summary: Cumulative excess withdrawals by the South Korean Interim Government reached a new high of 22,005 million won at the end of April, though only 2,146 million above six months earlier. April withdrawals were 2,340 million against 1,555 million deposits. Spending controls and higher utility, transport, tax and tobacco rates limited growth; total overdrafts were 39,325 million.

sections.title: Expenditure Budget of the South Korean Interim Government
sections.summary: The approved F/Y 1947/48 budget was 21,407 million won, with 787,000,000 won added in April and 1,177 million pending (Electra Barge, Communications, Police, Transportation, Justice), totaling 23,370 million. The Budget Bureau's F/Y 1948/49 recommendations total 28,704,824 thousand won expenditure against 27,821,485 thousand revenue; agencies may spend one-twelfth in April while the National Economic Board reviews.

sections.title: Monthly Revenues and Expenditures
sections.summary: March revenues of 2,135 million won set a monthly record, 507 million above February. Monopoly Bureau receipts reached 1,004 million won, tax collections 432 million, and departmental revenue nearly 700 million, helped by 520 million from Transportation. Expenditures rose 601 million won over February but stayed below the six-month average; Table 5 gives monthly series.

sections.title: Ratios Between Revenues and Expenditures
sections.summary: Cumulative F/Y 1947/48 revenue (15,336 million won, led by the Monopoly Bureau at 7,294 million) was 79 per cent of expenditure payments (19,319 million), 69 per cent of the proposed expenditure budget, while payments equalled 87 per cent of that budget. Tables 6 and 7 list revenues and expenditures by agency.

sections.title: Monopoly Bureau
sections.summary: Monopoly Bureau expenditures for March were 195.5 million won and 3,539 million for the fiscal year, mostly tobacco (2,698 million). Revenue for the year was 7,294 million won. Tobacco supplies about 10,000 of 28,000 million won estimated revenue (36 per cent); salt and ginseng add six and two per cent.

sections.title: Civilian Supply Program
sections.summary: The Civilian Supply Program sells goods bought by Military Government from Japan and the United States through South Korean Interim Government channels. Table 8 shows receipts and disbursements from May 1946; the balance stood at 5,319 million won at end of April 1948. Accounts receivable of 13,686 million won were also outstanding.

sections.title: Section 2: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Deposits in financial institutions rose 11% in April; loans, insurance and institution activities.

sections.title: Cash Balances in Financial Institutions
sections.summary: Cash balances in financial institutions rose 1,088 million won in March to 3,508.9 million, partly from reduced loans and higher deposits and partly as a rebound from February's fall. South Korea has no securities markets and banks face no legal liquid-reserve requirement. Table 1 gives balances from December 1946.

sections.title: Deposits in Financial Institutions
sections.summary: Deposit balances in financial institutions rose 6,279 million won, nearly 13 per cent, to a record 55,305 million in March; deposits were up 7,961 million and withdrawals down 1,500 million from February. Government balances grew nearly 1,900 million to 28,926 million, and inter-bank balances rose 1,159 million to a new high of 4,151 million.

sections.title: Deposit Balances in Each Financial Institution
sections.summary: Public deposits were the largest since December 1947, with balances up 3,221 million won to a record 22,228 million. Every type of deposit rose at every institution in March. Government deposits gained mainly at the Bank of Chosun, and inter-bank gains were at Chosun Industrial, Savings and Mutual Aid banks. Table 3 gives totals of 55,305 million.

sections.title: Loans by Financial Institutions
sections.summary: March was the third straight month in which loans retired exceeded new loans; outstanding loans fell 1,591 million won, nearly five per cent, to 32,120 million (guaranteed down 863 million, others 728 million). The Bank of Chosun held 30 per cent of loans; total loans equalled 58 per cent of deposits, with ratios per bank given.

sections.title: Life Insurance
sections.summary: Life insurance continued steady growth: insurance in force rose 74.4 million won, nine per cent, in March to 814.6 million. Premiums collected were 68 per cent above February and equalled 21 per cent of annual premiums due, while claims paid were the highest since January 1948. Four companies reported; a postal life insurance system also operates.

sections.title: Damage Insurance
sections.summary: Damage insurance companies wrote 9,265 new policies in March, fewer than January or February but well above the 1947 monthly average. Liabilities assumed of nearly 4,400 million won set a record, 42 per cent above February, and premiums written reached 51.6 million. Claims paid were exceeded only in January 1948.

sections.title: Life and Damage Insurance Activities
sections.summary: In April damage insurance companies were instructed to limit investments to first mortgages, real estate and corporate bonds and stocks, bank deposits and Korean Government obligations. A new life insurance salary scale, agreed after conferences between employees and companies, raised maximum salaries about 50 per cent; employees agreed to help improve operating efficiency.

sections.title: Activities of Financial Institutions
sections.summary: The new Bank Examination Section of the Department of Finance examined its first Korean bank and plans annual examinations on U.S. methods. Controller of Commodities proposed repaying the 12,502 million won rice loan by 31 October (4,540 million repaid). Ordinance 182 replaced Japanese-printed 100 won notes, about 5,000 million exchanged at 75 million cost. Thirty-nine loans totalling 713 million won were approved, including 400 million for the Irrigation Union.

sections.title: Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Administration, legislature, politics, legal affairs, police and interzone activities.

sections.title: Section 1: Administration
sections.summary: Election preparations (7,730,000 registered, 942 candidates), National Economic Board and Military Government personnel.

sections.title: Preparation for National Election
sections.summary: Registration closed 9 April with 7,730,000 voters, over 94 per cent of those eligible (51 per cent men); 200 districts and 13,407 polling places were set, and 942 candidates registered. Public Information publicised the election via press releases, Hodge, Jacobs and Dean statements, directives prioritising trials of election interference, posed pictures, 100 film shorts and radio coverage.

sections.title: National Economic Board
sections.summary: The National Economic Board met seven times and reviewed F/Y 1948/49 budgets. It discussed an agricultural production tax, authorised 400 million won credit for the Korean Irrigation Union, passed 250 million for the Sumjingang Dam power project, and approved summer grain collection of at least 20 per cent of output. It centralised funds in the Bank of Chosun and listed its publications.

sections.title: Military Government Personnel
sections.summary: Military Government personnel numbered 3,041 in April 1948 (547 officers, 1,469 enlisted men, 1,025 civilians), up from 2,740 in March. Table 1 shows military strength steady and civilians rising for seven months, while civilian turnover was high because of one-year contracts. The total was 3,721 in October 1946.

sections.title: Section 2: Korean Interim Legislative Assembly
sections.summary: KILA met once on 19 April, enacted nothing, and voted 30-day adjournment amounting to dissolution; summary of legislation.

sections.title: April Session
sections.summary: The Korean Interim Legislative Assembly met only once in April, on the 19th, and enacted no legislation. It rejected resignations of Yun Ki-sop, Kim Ik-tong and Lee Sun-taek to keep membership at 49, tabled pending bills until the National Assembly convenes, and adjourned 30 days, tantamount to dissolution.

sections.title: Summary of KILA Legislation
sections.summary: KILA, first proposed June 1946 and convened 12 December 1946 with 45 elected and 45 appointed members, passed 11 Public Acts (including child labor, rice and grain collection, abolition of licensed prostitution, Arbor Day) and four resolutions. It nearly dissolved three times: the May 1947 voting-age dispute, the November 1947 outline of measures, and the January-February 1948 UN petition.

sections.title: Section 3: Political Developments
sections.summary: North-South Conference at Pyongyang from 19 April, election candidacies and land reform.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Two matters absorbed South Korean parties in April: the Pyongyang North-South conference opening 19 April, and the first general election. Over 90 per cent of eligible voters registered, and 939 candidates sought 200 National Assembly seats when registration closed 16 April. Moderates and communists focused on the conference, rightists on the election.

sections.title: North-South Conference
sections.summary: Party reactions split: moderates and leftists backed the conference, while Hankook Democratic Party and Rhee opposed it. Kim Koo and Kimm Kiu-sic, hesitant at first, went to Pyongyang. Sessions from 19 April were scripted; a 23 April resolution demanded foreign troop withdrawal, and a 30 April communique rejected the separate election. The report judges it a Soviet victory.

sections.title: Election Preparations
sections.summary: Rightists formed an election acceleration committee under O Sei-chang; 939 candidates, 17 of them women, contested 200 seats allotted by province, with Rhee's society fielding 239 and Dai Dong 89. Party splits and a poll claiming 91 per cent were forced to register appeared. Choi Nung-chin's challenge to Rhee in Tongdaimoon A was nullified 7 May.

sections.title: Land Reform
sections.summary: Extreme rightists, backed largely by landlords, opposed the National Land Administration's sale of New Korea Company land to tenants, saying the property was Korean and should be disposed of by a Korean government. Communists accused U.S. authorities of keeping proceeds and wanted free distribution as in North Korea. Non-extremists generally favored the sales.

sections.title: Section 4: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Executive Orders including election date moved to 10 May; legal opinions, penal institutions, codification of civil code.

sections.title: Ordinances and Orders
sections.summary: April ordinances included Executive Order 20 moving the election to 10 May because of an eclipse, Order 21 on demonstrations and liquor, and Ordinances 182-191 (banknote exchange, repeal of obsolete laws, port fees, income tax exemption raised to 25,000 won). Hodge proclaimed 11 rights of Koreans on 5 April and a 10 May holiday; KILA's last act was Public Act 11.

sections.title: Legal Opinions
sections.summary: Department of Justice opinions covered: no licence needed for foreign firms such as Jardine, Matheson to trade; English as official language of the National Land Administration; implied licensing power over film distribution; informal adoption under customary law allowing a Seoul adoption agency; and National Food Administration being independent of the National Economic Board.

sections.title: Penal Institutions
sections.summary: Prisons were guarded against election-time release attempts, and six were found in good condition. Kunchon Prison became an adult institution taking about 200 overflow prisoners, and prisoners worked for Army units. The Kaesong Boys' Reformatory, holding 1,100 boys aged 14 to 20, was praised for its buildings, discipline rules, schooling, five trade shops and Warden Kwon Yung-jun.

sections.title: Court Liaison
sections.summary: Release of prisoners under the Military Governor's amnesty was completed in April, except for some transferred prisoners who were being traced. Delivery of pardon-order copies to many paroled or suspended-sentence persons was impossible because their addresses were unknown.

sections.title: Property Claims Commission
sections.summary: The Department of Justice adviser and the Property Custodian recommended transferring to the Custodian pending claims with abundant proof of Korean ownership, and the Property Claims Commission concurred. The Custodian will release such property administratively, speeding relief for Korean claimants suffering hardship from loss of their property.

sections.title: Codification Bureau
sections.summary: A proposed Civil Code, drafted by Judge C. Sumner Lobingier, was finished and being translated; it will be Korea's first, replacing the untranslated Japanese code. Lobingier's reasons, the placing of corporation law under juristic persons, his Chinese and European sources, and the four-book syllabus (Persons, Obligations, Property, Succession) are given.

sections.title: Section 5: National Police
sections.summary: Court-warrant rule worked; communist violence aimed at registration, with about 52 attacks on 13,455 booths.

sections.title: Reform Measures
sections.summary: A court-warrant requirement for arrests began to work more smoothly than expected, though police had feared it would block precautionary arrests. Police also felt they lost face when over 3,000 minor political offenders were released and resented limits on harshness and property destruction, balking at signing statements justifying force.

sections.title: Violence
sections.summary: Communist-inspired violence aimed to block registration: about 52 of 13,455 booths were attacked, led by Kyongsang-pukto with 21. Attacks on police and sabotage fell, but bystander injuries and disorders rose, with savage killings. Cheju-do's outbreak from 3 April involved about 2,000 rioters; to 19 April, 22 civilians and seven police were killed.

sections.title: Warning
sections.summary: There were signs that communists were renewing efforts to win adherents among security forces. Police were told that the Americans were on their way out and the communists coming in, so it would be wise to join the winning side.

sections.title: Section 6: Interzone Activities
sections.summary: Weekly North-South mail exchange (59,000 pieces), Radio Pyongyang intercepts and border incidents.

sections.title: Mail Exchange
sections.summary: Mail exchange between North and South Korea became weekly from 15 April. Four exchanges in April handled 59,000 pieces versus 37,000 in March, counted as regular mail, postcards and registered items. The largest was 3 April, with 9,768 letters, 3,313 postcards and 703 registered items from South Korea.

sections.title: Radio Pyongyang Intercepts
sections.summary: Radio Pyongyang used the Joint Conference to attack the South's separate election, praise the 1947 People's Economic Plan, and denounce Rhee, American colonisation and South Korean land sales. Kim Il-sung's opening speech was the month's key broadcast. The People's Assembly adopted a constitution 28-30 April, subject to an all-Korean assembly's approval.

sections.title: Border Incidents
sections.summary: Police Director Chough Pyong-ok said 38th parallel incidents reached a new high, with uniformed Soviet soldiers accompanying communist raids in at least two cases. Since 7 February, 21 Koreans were killed and about 150 wounded, and North Korean marauders violated the border 74 times. Small-arms fire echoes across the parallel nightly.

sections.title: Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Public health, education, culture, press, youth and women.

sections.title: Section 1: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Mukden repatriate teams, cholera vaccine distribution, nurse training, lepers, narcotics, laboratories and public assistance.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Public Health and Welfare expanded training and disease control, outfitting the refugee ship that repatriated Koreans from Mukden via Tientsin with welfare and preventive medicine teams. Medical Services ran training courses and Nursing launched a graduate nurse program. Cholera vaccine and control supplies went to the provinces for the three-phase vaccination.

sections.title: Preventive Medicine
sections.summary: Communicable disease stayed low, with typhus and typhoid declining. Cholera and smallpox immunisation covered seacoast cities, border refugee camp towns and border townships. The National Health Center milk station served 120 infants daily. The Mukden refugee ship sailed 30 April with a 14-day quarantine planned. A Pusan quarantine property dispute was settled and a vital statistics course held.

sections.title: Medical Services
sections.summary: The last UNRRA medical shipment, worth about $2,000, was divided among four leprosaria at Yosu, Sorakto, Taegu and Pusan. The tenth class for doctors and x-ray technicians at the Lasan Tuberculosis Sanitorium finished, bringing the total completing courses to 50.

sections.title: Nursing Affairs
sections.summary: A three-month training program for graduate nurses began 1 April at three U.S. Army hospitals under the 80th Medical Group. Surplus Army nurses' clothing was arranged for sale to Korean hospitals. Inspections found Pusan Transportation Hospital poor, Pusan City Hospital much improved, and Seoul City Hospital lacking adequate nursing care.

sections.title: Veterinary Affairs
sections.summary: Completed statistics for 1946 and 1947 showed more animals treated in 1947, with cattle rising from 26,302 to 34,591 and recoveries 97 per cent, helped by imported supplies. The fifth veterinary bulletin on horse breeding was distributed, 400 copies via the Department of Agriculture and 160 by Agriculture Improvement Service.

sections.title: Pharmaceutical Affairs
sections.summary: Military Government received 520,000 pounds of DDT in April, distributed through Army Malaria Control Units in each province. The first large shipment of 100,000 bars of laundry and toilet soap went to hospitals, doctors and dentists. Of 44 candidates in the spring pharmacists' examination, only two completed all three parts.

sections.title: Narcotics Section
sections.summary: After investigation, the Narcotics Section licensed 74 physicians and 31 pharmacists to handle narcotics in April. The Narcotics Adviser and section chief inspected the narcotics ward at Sun Hwa Hospital, Seoul, and interviewed six addicts under treatment.

sections.title: Laboratories
sections.summary: The National Vaccine Laboratory in Seoul kept production of biologicals at requirements, and increased cholera, typhoid and rabies vaccine output. Smallpox vaccine production was delayed because of budgetary difficulties.

sections.title: Public Assistance
sections.summary: A flood-season disaster relief plan relies on local community organisations for food, clothing and shelter. Welfare officers completed 10,053 low-cost housing units, and five child welfare institutions were licensed; UNRRA aid of 300,000 won went to White Lily Orphanage. The Kaesong Refugee Camp processes 500 to 1,000 North Korean refugees, with relief agencies supplying clothing.

sections.title: Section 2: Education
sections.summary: Adult literacy rose, curriculum workshops, first model hospital ward, and bureau activities.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Curriculum workshops in art, music, science, home economics and English grew in number and drew many teachers. A nursing radio program began, and the Medical Section arranged South Korea's first model hospital ward. Surveys indicated the adult education program greatly reduced adult illiteracy through local schools, radio and press.

sections.title: Bureau of Research and Special Subjects
sections.summary: The program stressed democratic community education, and tables showed literacy rising from 21 per cent in August 1945 to 71 per cent in August 1947. Higher education grew from 19 to 26 schools and 3,039 to 19,241 students. Adult schools reached 15,502 by September 1947. A middle-school entrance achievement test with four forms was prepared.

sections.title: Special Activities
sections.summary: The Department studied the acute situation of Korean schools in Japan; a Directorate sub-committee proposed reopening them with approved Korean textbooks and sending an investigating committee. A Personnel Ceiling Board cut the Department's table of organization from 177 to 143, prompting reorganization and a proposal to merge the Bureau of Culture into Social Education.

sections.title: Bureau of Administration
sections.summary: A 3,200,000 won budget request was cut to 2,200,000 won, excluding secondary schools, prompting redrafting of sub-agency budgets. A statistical summary of children, teachers, classrooms and funds showed 2,041 new classrooms built, yet classes average 95 children. Per-classroom cost was estimated at 710,000 won; 650,000 was allotted, and middle schools got 140,000.

sections.title: Bureau of Common Schools
sections.summary: Curriculum workshops for social studies (Taegu), language and art (Taegu) and science (Seoul) trained certified teachers to run provincial workshops. Plans included 10 English vacation institutes and a textbook workshop for 15 Seoul English teachers. Half of Seoul's middle schools had American volunteer English teachers. The exceptional children section held parents' classes and studied a Lighthouse project for the blind.

sections.title: Bureau of Teachers' Training
sections.summary: The Bureau prepared a booklet on teaching United Nations facts and social studies materials, and sent a draft Educators' Guide to Korea to Washington. A Chunju teachers' meeting drew 600 against the 200 expected. Preliminary plans for a normal-school summer session were estimated to train 10,000 elementary teachers.

sections.title: Bureau of Higher Education
sections.summary: Advisers helped develop a curriculum for Taegu Agriculture College. A Seoul National University Medical School committee decided on a model ward of about 30 beds. Two thousand nursing ethics textbooks were printed, and 19 nurses from the Seoul Electric Company hospital, the first run to American standards, completed refresher training.

sections.title: Bureau of Adult Education and Culture
sections.summary: The Bureau of Adult Education and Culture prepared a manuscript on the schools' responsibility in connection with the 10 May election and submitted it to the Department of Public Information for publication.

sections.title: Bureau of Textbooks
sections.summary: A total of 13,230,670 textbooks had been published since 15 August 1945, with April printings including Korean readers, Grade 6 social studies and Grade 6 science (678,500 copies). Work began to standardise mathematics, government and science works, and the first 7,000 English-language textbooks arrived, with sets for each middle school.

sections.title: American Language Institute
sections.summary: The American Language Institute began a new term on 26 April. At student request, the evening class for middle school English teachers will meet four times a week instead of twice. One thousand surplus library books from the Inchon salvage yard went to the Institute and normal schools.

sections.title: Bureau of Vocational Education
sections.summary: The adviser prepared a supplementary budget to set up a Korean Bureau of Vocational Education and considered converting the Department of Communications school into a model Seoul technical institute. A Korean Home Economics Association was organised, and field trips to Taegu and Kaesong found equipment shortages, broken sewing machines and food-cost problems.

sections.title: Section 3: Culture
sections.summary: Arbor Day tree planting (100 million trees), Symphony Orchestra instrument gift, music, dance, broadcasting and sports.

sections.title: Arbor Day
sections.summary: Arbor Day, 5 April, made a national holiday by Public Act No. 10, was marked on Nam San with about 10,000 participants. Military Governor Dean planted the first of 100,000,000 trees planted nationwide, five per person, and 26,000 trees covering 19 acres were planted on Nam San that afternoon.

sections.title: Korea Symphony Orchestra
sections.summary: On 25 April Lt.-Gen. Hodge presented musical instruments from U.S. personnel to the Korea Symphony Orchestra, a public corporation founded September 1945 with 30 musicians and now 60. A concert under Lim Won-sik included the first Korean performance of an American orchestral work, Douglas Moore's Village Music.

sections.title: Music and Dances
sections.summary: Music and dance events included a 28-29 April election publicity program by Seoul pupils, the 22d symphony concert under Kim In-soo, and recitals. Farmers performed the rain ceremonial dance on Nam San 4-10 April, an Oriental dance troupe performed 10-11 April, and a 17 April court music program for UNTCOK featured a mask dance.

sections.title: Other Cultural Activities
sections.summary: Thousands viewed cherry blossoms in mid-April, with 10,000 at the Zoological Gardens on 11 April. A "Night of Poets" at the YMCA on 25 April supported the Liberation of Korean Culture in Japan. Two commemorative stamps issued 10 April showed Independence Arch (20 won) and the turtle ship (50 won).

sections.title: Korea Broadcasting System
sections.summary: The Korea Broadcasting System publicised the election through spot announcements and programs such as the Adult Culture Hour, and ran a 52-student radio class at Ewha College. It recorded Korean songs for pressing in the United States, gave scripts to the Hoover Library, made two remote opera broadcasts, and favored Beethoven in evening music.

sections.title: Sports
sections.summary: Fifty-eight athletes were selected for Korea's team to the London Olympics, with 10 track and field men, 16 soccer players and nine basketball players. A lottery of 560,000 tickets raised funds to $140,000 by 24 April, averting a 35-man cut. Weightlifters broke six records, and Suh Yun-bok won the Boston-memorial marathon on 18 April.

sections.title: Section 4: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Press focused on election and Pyongyang conference; riots, law enforcement, amnesty of 3,140 and fear of Japan.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: The 10 May election and the 19-24 April Pyongyang Conference dominated the press. Voter registration, amnesty and disturbances were treated as phases of the election struggle. The closing of Korean schools in Japan was read by Koreans as a plot to re-enslave Korea and by American authorities as a communist scheme, and judicial and police reform were discussed in election terms.

sections.title: Pyongyang Conference
sections.summary: Pyongyang Conference coverage filled most newspaper space in early April. Rightist reporters visiting the Soviet-controlled city found liberties completely suppressed in North Korea, while leftist reporters found conditions perfect.

sections.title: Registration for Election
sections.summary: U.S. authorities worked to create a free atmosphere: papers printed Hodge's 2 April secret-ballot statement, the civil rights ordinance took effect 1 April, and an amnesty freed 3,140 political offenders. The UN Commission found people wanted unification. Both sides alleged intimidation; 52 of 13,455 centers were attacked. Kyeng Hyang Sin Mun reported 91.7 per cent registered.

sections.title: Political Campaign
sections.summary: Rightist papers complained of 939 candidates for 200 seats, with independents (including moderates and leftists whose parties boycotted the vote) making up 48 per cent; some non-recommended candidates withdrew under party commendation. Military Governor Dean's 8 April press conference denied High Commissioner, US-printed Bank of Chosun notes and land-sale charges; communists alleged colonization and puppet government.

sections.title: Law Enforcement
sections.summary: A police-initiated, Military Government-approved Fatherland Protection Group enlisted men aged 18 to 55 to curb election terrorism, with safeguards against a revival of the Japanese-era namesake. The Korean Supreme Court rejected American police advisers' 3 April petition on police-issued arrest warrants. Sentences of Chang Duk-soo's assassins were commuted on 23 April.

sections.title: Riots and Disorders
sections.summary: Disturbances in the southern provinces continued through April, with violent outbreaks on Cheju-do beginning 3-7 April. A police report cited 15 killed and 30 wounded; a rightist paper said the riots were worsening and that Constabulary Ninth Regiment troops were sent. A 29 April report described 2,000 armed men in mountain dugouts and martial law.

sections.title: Fear of Japan
sections.summary: Korean papers of all views protested the 31 March closing of Korean schools in Japan as an attack on Korean culture and independence, while printing General Dean's statement that the schools were communist training centers. Korean Education and Foreign Affairs offices urged SKIG-approved textbooks and punishment of Kobe rioters. The press also feared Japanese travel permits would revive militarism.

sections.title: Section 5: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: 67,475 members planted trees on Arbor Day; cleanup, training, vocational work, election preparation.

sections.title: Community Service
sections.summary: Government-sponsored Korean National Youth mobilized 67,475 members in all nine provinces on Arbor Day, 5 April, planting 3,451,300 trees in 1,086,880 working hours. The effort is part of an ongoing project: 1,246,480 trees planted in early 1948 versus 175,000 in all of 1947. Members also patrol forests and ran an April cleanup campaign, including 7,000 members at Inchon.

sections.title: Membership and Training
sections.summary: KNY membership reached 774,949 on 30 April 1948, including 108,326 women, growing by over 3,000 daily; tables give monthly totals since January 1947 and provincial breakdowns. Over 370,000 members joined in four months, with 1,000,000 forecast by 30 June. Seven new training centers brought the total to 62, and 36,599 leaders were trained in the first quarter.

sections.title: Vocational Training
sections.summary: KNY emphasized recruiting employed workers and training apprentices, countering the tradition of unemployed youths joining for strong-arm gain. On-the-job classes were organized in about six communication and transportation industries, and the national Department of Organization expanded job placement in April. At Yongdongpo, apprentices manufactured and assembled prefabricated homes to ease the provincial housing shortage.

sections.title: Election Preparations
sections.summary: During April thousands of KNY members across the American zone urged neighbors to vote in the 10 May election without backing any candidate or party. They held neighborhood sessions explaining the democratic concept of suffrage. In areas lacking government funds for transportation and salaries, members also distributed ballots and ballot boxes.

sections.title: Section 6: Women's Activities
sections.summary: Women's Bureau election education, press, sewing aids, YWCA, Junior Red Cross, KNY women, professional women; blank pages follow.

sections.title: The Women's Bureau
sections.summary: Election preparation was the Women's Bureau's main April work: over 50 speeches to girls' schools, colleges and community groups on suffrage, and a provincial tour with Civil Information staff showing the film "The Peoples Choice". Posters and leaflets urged registration. Its mothers' school averaged 80 attendees, 5,000 copies of "New Homemaking" were distributed, and two teachers assisted a hospital kitchen training program.

sections.title: The Women's Press
sections.summary: The "Women's Press", Korea's only women's newspaper, was published by Park Sun Chun, a Legislative Assembly candidate, and founded 21 April 1947 with 27 staff and 8,000 daily circulation. A two-page paper sponsored by the Women's Patriotic Society, its April editorials stressed the election; the 8 April editorial urged women to vote, citing 15,000,000 eligible women.

sections.title: Sewing Aids
sections.summary: Church women's groups in the United States sent several hundred dollars' worth of sewing aids to Korean women in April, handed to Korean welfare agencies for needy families. One family newly arrived from Manchuria used needles and thread to alter clothing supplied by Licensed Agencies for Relief of Asia, while others made quilts with LARA batting.

sections.title: Domestic Economy Science Association
sections.summary: The Domestic Economy Science Association, Korea's first home economics association, was organized in April by American adviser Mrs. Lyda Heffron at Shangshin Girls' Middle School, Seoul. It has 30 charter members, restricted to middle-school-level teachers and up, with only Seoul active. Its program covers publications, teaching-method research, and literature and reference collections on domestic economy.

sections.title: The YWCA
sections.summary: The National YWCA received $57,000 from American Overseas Aid for Adolescents and the UN Appeal for Children to feed 2,000 undernourished South Korean adolescents. An executive committee was appointed and principals of three Seoul primary schools consulted. Each school gets a feeding room and nurse, food and menus come from the YWCA, and Dr. Y.Y. Kim is examining physician.

sections.title: Junior Red Cross
sections.summary: The first members of the Korean Junior Red Cross were initiated at a Seoul ceremony in April led by chief Miss Kim On-hie and Seoul chapter chief Mrs. Chai Sun Pok. Its first project is spreading health knowledge through literature and hygiene aids, supported by 50,000 boxes of toilet articles from the American Junior Red Cross.

sections.title: Women of Korean National Youth
sections.summary: The KNY women's section, headed by former champion athlete Kim Hyun Suk and backed by the Aegug Puin, trains women for citizenship; 108,326 of 774,949 KNY members were women on 30 April. Training covers first aid, home nursing, child care and crafts under the principle "train before organizing"; 121 women graduated at Suwon in early 1948.

sections.title: Professional Women
sections.summary: Profiles highlight the Koh sisters: Evelyn (law degree from Doshisha, M.A. in economics at Michigan), Gladys (piano diploma, Ph.D. in absentia) and Dr. Nan (M.D., studying public health at Michigan). They ran the Chamawon "Sisters' Garden" settlement near Seoul. Evelyn now heads the Women's Bureau and Gladys directs Red Cross women's volunteer services.
